text.p: These are the leading stories in the Egyptian press on Sunday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
- Foreign Minister Amr Moussa will read President Hosni Mubarak's speech to the Islamic summit in Islamabad today.
- Mubarak met U.S. Deputy Defence Secretary John White. White has been to Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait and Israel and left Cairo yesterday.

- A report by an International Monetary Fund (IMF) mission to Egypt praised the performance of the government of Prime Minister Kamal Ganzouri, saying it had successfully carried out its economic reform programme.

- The ministerial group on privatisation, at a meeting yesterday under Ganzouri, approved a timetable for dealing with the state's stake in joint-venture banks and companies and a draft system of compensation for workers who give up their jobs voluntarily before the age of 60.
- Amr Moussa said that Egypt will not recognise any illegal changes in Jerusalem and that the settlement policy of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is not a good sign.
- Grand Sheikh of al-Azhar Mohamed Sayyed Tantawi said in the Nile Delta town of Tanta that the Israeli government is working for war and stirring up strife, not for a just and comprehensive peace.

- Four members of the stock exchange board have been appointed. They are Mustafa Oweiss for the central bank, Ahmed Kheireddin for the Capital Market Authority, Mohamed Sharnoubi from Banque Misr and Mohamed Hassan Hussein from National Bank of Egypt. On April 29 six members will be elected from among the brokerages.
- Ganzouri announced that at the session of parliament today he will give details of the disbursement of compensation for victims of the Gulf War.

- The IMF mission report says that the Egyptian economy is expected to grow five percent in the financial year 1996/7, which ends on June 30, that inflation will continue to fall, that the inflow of capital will continue, strengthening the balance of payments, that the budget deficit will remain under control at less than one percent of GDP, that the privatisation programme will be carried out successfully.
It says that the challenges are to complete the economic reform programme and to increase the country's capacity to absorb capital inflows.
